nodes.name: Generalized $n$-position $k$-color Mastermind
nodes.statement: At the start of the game, Codemaker chooses a secret code $z \in [k]^n$. In each round, Codebreaker guesses a string $x \in [k]^n$. Codemaker replies with the numbers $\eq(z,x):= |\{ i \in [n] \mid z_i=x_i\}|$ of positions in which her and Codebreaker's string coincide, and with $\pi(z,x)$, the number of additional pegs having the right color, but being in the wrong position. Formally, $\pi(z,x):=\max_{\rho \in S_n}|\{i \in [n] \mid z_{i}=x_{\rho(i)}\}|-\eq(z,x)$, where $S_n$ denotes the set of all permutations of the set $[n]$. In the original game, $\eq(z,x)$ is indicated by black answer-pegs, and $\pi(z,x)$ is indicated by white answer-pegs. Based on this and all previous answers, Codebreaker may choose his next guess. He ``wins'' the game if his guess equals Codemaker's secret code.
nodes.statement_short: Codebreaker must identify Codemaker's secret string $z\in[k]^n$ in as few guesses as possible, learning only the black/white answer-peg counts.

nodes.name: Answer functions $\eq(z,x)$ and $\pi(z,x)$
nodes.statement: Codemaker replies with the numbers $\eq(z,x):= |\{ i \in [n] \mid z_i=x_i\}|$ of positions in which her and Codebreaker's string coincide, and with $\pi(z,x)$, the number of additional pegs having the right color, but being in the wrong position. Formally, $\pi(z,x):=\max_{\rho \in S_n}|\{i \in [n] \mid z_{i}=x_{\rho(i)}\}|-\eq(z,x)$, where $S_n$ denotes the set of all permutations of the set $[n]$. In the original game, $\eq(z,x)$ is indicated by black answer-pegs, and $\pi(z,x)$ is indicated by white answer-pegs.
nodes.statement_short: Black pegs count positions where guess and code agree; white pegs count the additional right-color/wrong-position matches.

nodes.name: Black-pegs only Mastermind
nodes.statement: We should note that often, and partially also in this work, a black-pegs only variant is studied, in which Codemaker reveals $\eq(z,x)$ but not $\pi(z,x)$.

nodes.name: Knuth's five-guess strategy for 4-position 6-color Mastermind
nodes.statement: For the original 4-position 6-color version, \ifLongCites{\cite{Knuth77}}{Knuth~\cite{Knuth77}} has given a deterministic strategy that wins the game in at most five guesses. He also showed that no deterministic strategy has a 4-round guarantee.
conclusions: a deterministic strategy that wins the game in at most five guesses
no deterministic strategy has a 4-round guarantee

nodes.name: Information-theoretic lower bound attributed to Pierre Duchet
nodes.statement: He noted that a simple information-theoretic argument (attributed to Pierre Duchet) provides a lower bound of $\Omega(n \log k / \log n)$ for any $k=k(n)$.
conclusions: a lower bound of $\Omega(n \log k / \log n)$

nodes.name: Chv\'atal's optimality of random guessing for $k \le n^{1-\eps}$
nodes.statement: Extending the result\ifLongCites{~\cite{Erd63}}{~\cite{Erd63} of Erd\H os and R\'enyi} from $k=2$ to larger numbers of colors, he then showed that for any fixed $\eps > 0$, $n$ sufficiently large and $k \le n^{1-\eps}$, repeatedly asking random guesses until all but the secret code are excluded by the answers is an optimal Codebreaker strategy (up to constant factors). More specifically, using the probabilistic method and random guesses, he showed the existence of a \emph{deterministic non-adaptive} strategy for Codebreaker, that is, a set of $(2+\eps) n \frac{1+2 \log k}{\log (n/k)}$ guesses such that the answers uniquely determine any secret code Codemaker might have chosen (here and in the remainder, $\log n$ denotes the binary logarithm of $n$). These bounds hold even in the black-pegs only version of the game.
nodes.statement_short: For $k\le n^{1-\eps}$ random guessing is optimal up to constants, and a deterministic non-adaptive set of $(2+\eps)n(1+2\log k)/\log(n/k)$ guesses exists.
assumptions: for any fixed $\eps > 0$, $n$ sufficiently large and $k \le n^{1-\eps}$
conclusions: repeatedly asking random guesses until all but the secret code are excluded by the answers is an optimal Codebreaker strategy (up to constant factors)
a set of $(2+\eps) n \frac{1+2 \log k}{\log (n/k)}$ guesses such that the answers uniquely determine any secret code Codemaker might have chosen

nodes.name: Chv\'atal's adaptive strategy for $n \le k \le n^2$
nodes.statement: For $k$ between $n$ and $n^2$, Chv\'atal presented a deterministic adaptive strategy using $2n \log k +4n$ guesses. For $k = n$, this strategy does not need white answer-pegs.
conclusions: a deterministic adaptive strategy using $2n \log k +4n$ guesses
For $k = n$, this strategy does not need white answer-pegs

nodes.name: Chen--Cunha--Homer upper bound
nodes.statement: showed that for any $k \geq n$, $2n \lceil \log n \rceil+2n+\lceil k/n \rceil+2$ guesses suffice.
conclusions: $2n \lceil \log n \rceil+2n+\lceil k/n \rceil+2$ guesses suffice

nodes.name: Goodrich's black-peg upper bound
nodes.statement: proved an upper bound of $n \lceil \log k \rceil +\lceil(2-1/k)n\rceil+k$ for the number of guesses needed to win the Mastermind game with an arbitrary number $k$ of colors and black answer-pegs only.
assumptions: an arbitrary number $k$ of colors and black answer-pegs only
conclusions: an upper bound of $n \lceil \log k \rceil +\lceil(2-1/k)n\rceil+k$ for the number of guesses needed to win the Mastermind game

nodes.name: J\"ager--Peczarski upper bounds
nodes.statement: This was again improved by \ifLongCites{\cite{JaegerP11}}{J\"ager and Peczarski~\cite{JaegerP11}}, who showed an upper bound of $n \lceil \log n \rceil - n + k + 1$ for the case $k > n$ and $n \lceil \log k \rceil + k$ for the case $k \le n$.
conclusions: an upper bound of $n \lceil \log n \rceil - n + k + 1$ for the case $k > n$ and $n \lceil \log k \rceil + k$ for the case $k \le n$

nodes.name: Koyama--Lai average-case optimal strategy
nodes.statement: They gave a strategy that solves Mastermind in an expected number of about 4.34 guesses if the secret string is sampled uniformly at random from all $6^4$ possibilities, and they showed that this strategy is optimal.
assumptions: if the secret string is sampled uniformly at random from all $6^4$ possibilities
conclusions: a strategy that solves Mastermind in an expected number of about 4.34 guesses
this strategy is optimal

nodes.name: NP-hardness of Mastermind consistency (Stuckman--Zhang)
nodes.statement: showed that it is NP-hard to decide whether there exists a secret code consistent with a given sequence of queries and black- and white-peg answers.
conclusions: it is NP-hard to decide whether there exists a secret code consistent with a given sequence of queries and black- and white-peg answers

nodes.name: Viglietta's hardness for two colors and $\#$P-completeness
nodes.statement: showed that both hardness results apply also to the setting with only $k=2$ colors. In addition, he proved that \emph{counting} the number of consistent secret codes is $\#$P-complete.
conclusions: both hardness results apply also to the setting with only $k=2$ colors
\emph{counting} the number of consistent secret codes is $\#$P-complete

nodes.name: Doerr--Winzen memory-restricted Mastermind
nodes.statement: This inspired, among others, the result~\cite{DoerrW12} showing that a memory-restricted version of Mastermind (using only two rows of the board) can still be solved in $O(n / \log n)$ guesses when the number of colors is constant.
assumptions: when the number of colors is constant
conclusions: a memory-restricted version of Mastermind (using only two rows of the board) can still be solved in $O(n / \log n)$ guesses

nodes.name: Random guessing strategy
nodes.statement: Interestingly, a very simple guessing strategy suffices, namely asking random guesses until the answers uniquely determine the secret code.
nodes.statement_short: Repeatedly ask independent uniformly random guesses until the accumulated answers pin down the secret code.

nodes.name: Theorem 1 (adaptive black-peg strategy)
nodes.statement: For Mastermind with $n$ positions and $k=k(n)$ colors, the following holds. \begin{itemize} \item If $k= \Omega(n)$ then there exists a randomized winning strategy that uses black pegs only and needs an expected number of $O(n \log \log n + k)$ guesses. \item If $k= o(n)$ then there exists a randomized winning strategy that uses black pegs only and needs an expected number of $O\left(n \log \left(\frac{\log n}{\log (n/k)}\right)\right)$ guesses. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Black-peg Mastermind is winnable with an expected $O(n\log\log n+k)$ guesses when $k=\Omega(n)$, and $O(n\log(\log n/\log(n/k)))$ guesses when $k=o(n)$.
assumptions: For Mastermind with $n$ positions and $k=k(n)$ colors
conclusions: there exists a randomized winning strategy that uses black pegs only and needs an expected number of $O(n \log \log n + k)$ guesses
there exists a randomized winning strategy that uses black pegs only and needs an expected number of $O\left(n \log \left(\frac{\log n}{\log (n/k)}\right)\right)$ guesses

nodes.name: Absolute constants and the $k=n^{1-\delta}$ reformulation
nodes.statement: The $O$-notation in Theorem~\ref{thm:main} only hides absolute constants. Note that, setting $k=:n^{1-\delta}$, $\delta=\delta(n)$, the bound for $k=o(n)$ translates to $O(n\log(\delta^{-1}))$.

nodes.name: $k\leq n$ and $k,n$ powers of two
nodes.statement: As justified in Section~\ref{sec:preliminaries} below, we assume that $k\leq n$ and that both $k$ and $n$ are powers of two.

nodes.name: Zero-answer observation
nodes.statement: A simple but crucial observation is that when we query a string $x \in [k]^n$ and the answer $\eq(z,x)$ is 0 (recall that $z$ denotes Codemaker's secret color code), then we know that all queried colors are wrong for their respective positions; i.e., we have $z_i\neq x_i$ for all $i \in [n]$.
nodes.statement_short: A query answered $\eq(z,x)=0$ certifies that every queried color is wrong at its position.
assumptions: when we query a string $x \in [k]^n$ and the answer $\eq(z,x)$ is 0
conclusions: we know that all queried colors are wrong for their respective positions; i.e., we have $z_i\neq x_i$ for all $i \in [n]$

nodes.name: Candidate color sets $C_i$
nodes.statement: we maintain, for each position $i$, a set $C_i\subseteq[k]$ of colors that we still consider possible at position $i$
differentia: colors that we still consider possible at position $i$

nodes.name: $0$-blocks
nodes.statement: We will refer to blocks that contribute $0$ to $\eq(z,r)$ as \emph{$0$-blocks} in the following.

nodes.name: Coin-weighing problem with a spring scale
nodes.statement: Specifically, we are given $m$ coins of unknown integer weights and a spring scale. We can use the spring scale to determine the total weight of an arbitrary subset of coins in one weighing. Our goal is to identify the weight of every coin with as few weighings as possible.
nodes.statement_short: Determine the weight of every one of $m$ coins using as few subset weighings on a spring scale as possible.

nodes.name: Grebinski--Kucherov coin-weighing bound
nodes.statement: It follows from a coin-weighing result by \ifLongCites{\cite{grebinski-journal}}{Grebinski and Kucherov~\cite{grebinski-journal}} that $O(m/\log m)$ random queries (of the described block form, simulating the weighing of a random subset of coins) suffice to determine the contribution of each block to $\eq(z,r)$ with some positive probability.
nodes.statement_short: $O(m/\log m)$ random block queries already reveal every block's contribution to $\eq(z,r)$ with positive probability.
assumptions: $O(m/\log m)$ random queries (of the described block form, simulating the weighing of a random subset of coins)
conclusions: suffice to determine the contribution of each block to $\eq(z,r)$ with some positive probability

nodes.name: Total query count summed over all phases
nodes.statement: $$\sum_{j=1}^{\log k} O\left(\frac{n}{\log (4n/\left(\frac{k}{2^{j-1}} \right))}\right) \stackrel{k = n}= O(n) \sum_{j=1}^{\log n} \frac{1}{j+1} = O(n \log \log n) $$
nodes.statement_short: Summing $O(n/\log(4n/k'))$ over the $\log n$ phases telescopes to $O(n\log\log n)$ for $k=n$.

nodes.name: Why Algorithm 1 deviates from the sketch
nodes.statement: We remark that our precise strategy, Algorithm~\ref{algo:mastermind}, slightly deviates from this description. This is due to a technical issue with our argument once the number $k'$ of remaining colors drops below $C\log n$ for some $C>0$. Specifically, beyond this point the error bound we derive for a fixed position is not strong enough to beat a union bound over all $n$ positions. To avoid this issue, we stop our color reduction scheme before $k'$ becomes that small (for simplicity as soon as $k'$ is less than $\sqrt{n}$), and solve the remaining Mastermind problem by asking random queries from the remaining set $C_1\times \dots \times C_n$, as originally proposed by \ifLongCites{\cite{Erd63}}{Erd\H os and R\'enyi~\cite{Erd63}} and \ifLongCites{\cite{Chvatal83}}{Chv\'atal~\cite{Chvatal83}}.
nodes.statement_short: The color-reduction scheme is stopped once $k'<\sqrt n$ because below $C\log n$ the per-position error bound no longer beats the union bound.

nodes.name: Determining a dummy color for every position
nodes.statement: We begin by determining a dummy color for each position, i.e., a color that we know to be wrong at that particular position. For this we simply query the $n+1$ many strings $(1,1, \dots, 1), (2,1,1, \dots, 1), \dots, (2, 2, \dots, 2)\in [k]^n$. Processing the answers to these queries in order, it is not hard to determine the location of all $1$'s and $2$'s in Codemaker's secret string $z$. In particular, this provides us with a dummy color for each position.
nodes.statement_short: The $n+1$ queries $(1,\dots,1),(2,1,\dots,1),\dots,(2,\dots,2)$ locate all $1$'s and $2$'s in $z$, yielding a dummy color at every position.
assumptions: we simply query the $n+1$ many strings $(1,1, \dots, 1), (2,1,1, \dots, 1), \dots, (2, 2, \dots, 2)\in [k]^n$
conclusions: it is not hard to determine the location of all $1$'s and $2$'s in Codemaker's secret string $z$
this provides us with a dummy color for each position

nodes.name: Dummy color
nodes.statement: a dummy color for each position, i.e., a color that we know to be wrong at that particular position
differentia: a color that we know to be wrong at that particular position

nodes.name: Reduction to $n$ and $k$ powers of two
nodes.statement: Next we argue that for the main part of our argument we may assume that $n$ and $k$ are powers of two. To see this for $n$, note that we can simply extend Codemaker's secret string in an arbitrary way such that its length is the smallest power of two larger than $n$, and pretend we are trying to determine this extended string. To get the answers to our queries in this extended setting, we just need to add the contribution of the self-made extension part (which we determine ourselves) to the answers Codemaker provides for the original string. As the extension changes $n$ at most by a factor of two, our claimed asymptotic bounds are unaffected by this. To argue that we may also assume $k$ to be a power of two, we make use of the dummy colors we already determined for the original value of $k$. Similar to the previous argument, we increase $k$ to the next power of two and consider the game with this larger number of colors. To get the answers to our queries in this extended setting from Codemaker (who still is in the original setting), it suffices to replace every occurrence of a color that is not in the original color set with the dummy color at the respective position.
nodes.statement_short: Padding $n$ to the next power of two and mapping surplus colors to dummy colors costs at most a factor two.
conclusions: we may assume that $n$ and $k$ are powers of two

nodes.name: Reduction to $k\leq n$
nodes.statement: We may and will also assume that $k\leq n$. If $k>n$ we can trivially reduce the number of colors to $n$ by making $k$ monochromatic queries. With this observation the first part of Theorem~\ref{thm:main} follows immediately from the $O(n\log\log n)$ bound we prove for the case $k=n$.
nodes.statement_short: $k$ monochromatic queries reduce any $k>n$ to $k=n$, so the first part of Theorem 1 follows from the $k=n$ case.
conclusions: we can trivially reduce the number of colors to $n$ by making $k$ monochromatic queries

nodes.name: Phase
nodes.statement: our strategy operates in \emph{phases}, where in the $j$th phase we reduce the sizes of the sets $C_i$ from $k/2^{j-1}$ to $k/2^j$

nodes.name: $|C_i|$ is not allowed to drop below $k/2^j$ in phase $j$
nodes.statement: For technical reasons, we do not allow the sizes of $C_i$ to drop below $k/2^j$ during phase $j$; i.e., once we have $|C_i|=k/2^j$ for some position $i\in[n]$, we no longer remove colors from $C_i$ at that position and ignore any information that would allow us to do so.

nodes.name: Round
nodes.statement: Each phase is divided into a large number of \emph{rounds}, where a round consists of querying a random string $r$ and subsequently identifying the $0$-blocks (blocks that contribute $0$ to $\eq(z,r)$) by the coin-weighing argument outlined above.
differentia: a round consists of querying a random string $r$ and subsequently identifying the $0$-blocks

nodes.name: Sampling set $\cR_j$
nodes.statement: at the beginning of phase $j$ we define the set $\cR_j:=C_1\times \dots \times C_n$, and sample the random string $r$ uniformly at random from $\cR_j$ in each round of phase $j$

nodes.name: Blocks $B_s$ and their contributions $v_s$
nodes.statement: As before we let $k'~:=~k/2^{j-1}$ and partition the $n$ positions into $m := 4 n / k'$ blocks of size $k'/4$. More formally, for every $s \in [m]$ we let $B_s := \{ (s-1) k'/4 +1, \dots, s k'/4 \}$ denote the indices of block $s$, and we denote by $v_s: = | \{ i \in B_s : z_i = r_i \} |$ the contribution of block $B_s$ to $\eq(z,r)$.
nodes.statement_short: The $n$ positions are cut into $m=4n/k'$ blocks $B_s$ of size $k'/4$, with $v_s$ the number of correct guesses inside block $s$.

nodes.name: Coin-weighing query $r_y$
nodes.statement: For $y \in \{0,1\}^m$, define $r_y$ as the query that is identical to $r$ on the blocks $B_s$ for which $y_s = 1$, and identical to the string of dummy colors on all other blocks.
nodes.statement_short: $r_y$ copies $r$ on the blocks selected by $y$ and uses dummy colors elsewhere, so its score weighs exactly that subset of blocks.
differentia: identical to $r$ on the blocks $B_s$ for which $y_s = 1$
identical to the string of dummy colors on all other blocks

nodes.name: Identifying block contributions is a coin-weighing problem
nodes.statement: Thus $\eq(z,r_y) = \sum_{s \in [m], y_s = 1} v_s$. With this observation, identifying the values $v_s$ from a set of queries of form $r_y$ is equivalent to a coin-weighing problem in which we have $m$ coins with positive integer weights that sum up to $\eq(z,r)$: Querying $r_y$ in the Mastermind game provides exactly the information we obtain from weighing the set of coins indicated by $y$.
nodes.statement_short: Querying $r_y$ returns exactly the total weight of the coin subset indicated by $y$, so recovering the $v_s$ is a coin-weighing instance.
conclusions: identifying the values $v_s$ from a set of queries of form $r_y$ is equivalent to a coin-weighing problem in which we have $m$ coins with positive integer weights that sum up to $\eq(z,r)$

nodes.name: The coin-weighing query count $f(m)=\Theta(m/\log m)$
nodes.statement: The function $f(m)$ is implicit in the proof of the coin-weighing result of~\cite{grebinski-journal}; it is in $\Theta(m/\log m)$ and guarantees that the coin-weighing succeeds with probability at least $1/2$.
assumptions: $f(m)$ of strings of form $r_y$, with $y\in\{0,1\}^m$ sampled uniformly at random (u.a.r.) and independently
conclusions: it is in $\Theta(m/\log m)$ and guarantees that the coin-weighing succeeds with probability at least $1/2$

nodes.name: At least half of the blocks are $0$-blocks
nodes.statement: Note that the inequality $\eq(z,r)\leq m/2$ also guarantees that at least half of the $m$ blocks are $0$-blocks.
conclusions: at least half of the $m$ blocks are $0$-blocks

nodes.name: Successful round
nodes.statement: We say that a round is \emph{successful} if $\eq(z,r) \leq m/2$ and if the coin-weighing successfully identifies all $0$-blocks.

nodes.name: Cost of the final random-guessing stage
nodes.statement: It follows from \ifLongCites{\cite{Chvatal83}}{Chv\'atal's result~\cite{Chvatal83}} that the expected number of queries needed for this is $O(n \log k' / \log (n/k'))= O(n)$.
assumptions: we simply ask queries sampled uniformly and independently at random from the current set
conclusions: the expected number of queries needed for this is $O(n \log k' / \log (n/k'))= O(n)$

nodes.name: Algorithm 1: Playing Mastermind with many colors
nodes.statement: Determine a dummy color for each position\; \lForEach{$i\in[n]$}{$C_i\assign[k]$\;} $j \assign 0$ and $k'\assign k$\; \While{$k' > \sqrt{n}$}{ $j \assign j+1$, $k' \assign k/2^{j-1}$, $\cR_j \assign C_1\times \dots \times C_n$, and $m \assign 4n/k'$\; \Repeat{$\forall i\in [n]: |C_i|= k'/2$}{ Select a string $r$ u.a.r.\ from $\cR_j$ and query $\eq(z,r)$\; \If{$\eq(z,r)\leq m/2$ }{ \For{$i=1, \ldots, f(m)$ \quad /* $f(m) = \Theta(m/\log m)$ /* } {Sample $y$ u.a.r.\ from $\{0,1\}^m$ and query $\eq(z,r_y)$\;} \If{\normalfont{these $f(m)$ queries determine the $0$-blocks of $r$}}{ \ForEach{$i\in[n]$} {\lIf{\normalfont{$i$ is in a $0$-block and $|C_i|> k'/2$}} {$C_i \assign C_i\setminus\{r_i\}$\;} } } } } } $\cR \assign C_1\times \dots \times C_n$\; Select strings $r$ independently and u.a.r.\ from $\cR$ and query $\eq(z,r)$ until $z$ is determined\;
nodes.statement_short: Halve every candidate set $C_i$ phase by phase -- random query $r$, then $\Theta(m/\log m)$ coin-weighing queries to spot the $0$-blocks -- and finish by random guessing once $k'<\sqrt n$.

nodes.name: Claim 2 (expected number of rounds in a phase)
nodes.statement: The expected number of rounds required to complete phase $j$ is $O(k')=O(k/2^j)$.
conclusions: The expected number of rounds required to complete phase $j$ is $O(k')=O(k/2^j)$

nodes.name: Expected number of rounds $\mathbb E[T]$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \mathbb E[T] = \sum_{t \ge 1} \Pr[ T \ge t ] \le 16k' + n \sum_{t > 16k'} e^{-ct} = 16k' + n e^{-\Omega(k')}= O(k'), \end{equation}

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 2
nodes.statement: We first show that a round is successful with probability at least $1/4$. Recall that $\eq(z,r)$ has an expected value of $n/k'=m/4$. Thus, by Markov's inequality, we have $\eq(z,r)\leq m/2$ with probability at least $1/2$. Moreover, as already mentioned, the proof of the coin-weighing result by \ifLongCites{\cite{grebinski-journal}}{Grebinski and Kucherov~\cite{grebinski-journal}} implies that our $f(m)=\Theta(m/\log m)$ random coin-weighing queries identify all $0$-blocks with probability at least $1/2$. Thus, in total the probability for a successful round is at least $1/2\cdot 1/2=1/4$. We continue by showing that the probability that a successful round decreases the number of available colors for a fixed position, say position 1, is at least $1/4$. Note that this happens if $r \in \cR_j$ satisfies the following two conditions: \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] $v_1=0$, i.e., block $B_1$ is a 0-block with respect to $r$, and \item[(ii)] $r_1\in C_1$, i.e., the color $r_1$ has not been excluded from $C_1$ in a previous round of phase $j$. \end{itemize} For (i) recall that in a successful round at least $m/2$ of the $m$ blocks are $0$-blocks. It follows by symmetry that $B_1$ is a 0-block with probability at least $1/2$. Moreover, conditional on (i), $r_1$ is sampled uniformly at random from the $k'-1$ colors that are different from $z_1$ and were in $C_1$ at the beginning of the round. Thus the probability that $r_1$ is in the current set $C_1$ is $|C_1|/(k'-1)$, which is at least $1/2$ because we do not allow $|C_1|$ to drop below $k'/2$. We conclude that, conditional on a successful round, the random query $r$ decreases $|C_1|$ by one with probability at least $1/2\cdot 1/2=1/4$. Thus, in total, the probability that a round decreases $|C_1|$ by one is at least $1/4\cdot 1/4=1/16$ throughout our strategy. It follows that the probability that after $t$ successful rounds in phase $j$ we still have $|C_1|>k'/2$ is bounded by the probability that in $t$ independent Bernoulli trials with success probability $1/16$ we observe fewer than $k'/2$ successes. If $t/16\geq k'$, by Chernoff bounds this probability is bounded by $e^{-ct}$ for some absolute constant $c>0$. Let us now denote the number of rounds phase $j$ takes by the random variable $T$. By a union bound, the probability that $T\geq t$, i.e., that after $t$ steps at one of the positions $i\in[n]$ we still have $|C_i|>k'/2$, is bounded by $ne^{-ct}$ for $t\geq 16k'$. It follows that \begin{equation} \mathbb E[T] = \sum_{t \ge 1} \Pr[ T \ge t ] \le 16k' + n \sum_{t > 16k'} e^{-ct} = 16k' + n e^{-\Omega(k')}= O(k'), \end{equation} where the last step is due to $k'\geq \sqrt{n}=\omega(\log n)$.
nodes.statement_short: Markov plus the coin-weighing guarantee give success probability $1/4$ per round; a Chernoff bound and a union bound over positions then give $\mathbb E[T]=O(k')$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: Recall that for each phase $j$ we have $m=\Theta(n/k')=\Theta(n/(k/2^{j-1}))$ and that $f(m)=\Theta(m/\log m)$. Thus by Claim~\ref{claim:one-phase}, the expected number of queries our strategy asks in phase $j$ is bounded by $$O(k')\cdot (1 + f(m)) = O\left(\frac{n}{\log(\frac{n}{k/2^j})}\right) = O\left( \frac{n}{\log(n/k) +j}\right).$$ It follows that throughout the main part of our strategy we ask an expected number of queries of at most $$O(n) \sum_{j=1}^{\log k} \frac{1}{\log(n/k) +j} = O\big(n \big(\log \log n - \log\log (n/k)\big)\big)= O\left(n \log \left(\frac{\log n}{\log (n/k)}\right)\right). $$ (This calculation is for $k<n$; as observed before, for $k=n$ a very similar calculation yields a bound of $O(n\log\log n)$.) As the number of queries for determining the dummy colors and for wrapping up at the end is only $O(n)$, Theorem~\ref{thm:main} follows.
nodes.statement_short: Multiply the $O(k')$ rounds per phase by the $1+f(m)$ queries per round and sum the harmonic-type series over all phases.

nodes.name: Theorem 3 (deterministic polynomial-time strategy)
nodes.statement: The bounds stated in Theorem~\ref{thm:main} can be achieved by a deterministic winning strategy. Furthermore, this winning strategy can be realized in polynomial time.
conclusions: can be achieved by a deterministic winning strategy
this winning strategy can be realized in polynomial time

nodes.name: Grebinski--Kucherov distinguishing set of coin-weighing queries
nodes.statement: They showed that a set of $f'(m)= \Theta(m/\log m)$ random coin-weighing queries $y^1, \ldots, y^{f'(m)}$, sampled from $\{0,1\}^m$ independently and uniformly at random, has, with some positive probability, the property that it distinguishes any two distinct coin-weighing instances in the following sense: For any two distinct vectors $v, w$ with non-negative integer entries such that $\sum_{s\in[m]}{v_s} \leq m/2$ and $\sum_{s\in[m]}{w_s} \leq m/2$, there exists an index $j\in[f'(m)]$ for which $\sum_{s\in[m],y^j_s=1}{v_s}\neq\sum_{s\in[m],y^j_s=1}{w_s}$.
nodes.statement_short: With positive probability $\Theta(m/\log m)$ random $0/1$ query vectors separate every pair of distinct coin-weight vectors of total weight $\le m/2$.
assumptions: For any two distinct vectors $v, w$ with non-negative integer entries such that $\sum_{s\in[m]}{v_s} \leq m/2$ and $\sum_{s\in[m]}{w_s} \leq m/2$
conclusions: there exists an index $j\in[f'(m)]$ for which $\sum_{s\in[m],y^j_s=1}{v_s}\neq\sum_{s\in[m],y^j_s=1}{w_s}$

nodes.name: Bshouty's polynomial-time coin-weighing algorithm
nodes.statement: An algorithm for doing the latter is given in the work of \ifLongCites{\cite{Bshouty09}}{Bshouty~\cite{Bshouty09}}.
nodes.statement_short: A polynomial-time solver for the coin-weighing subproblems, used as a black box to make the whole strategy polynomial-time.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3
nodes.statement: The main loop of the algorithm described above uses randomization in two places: for generating the random string $r$ of each round (line~\ref{line:sample} in Algorithm 1), and for generating the $f(m)$ many random coin-weighing queries $r_y$ used to identify the $0$-blocks of $r$ if $\eq(z,r)\leq m/2$ (line~\ref{line:coins2}). The derandomization of the coin-weighing algorithm is already given in the work of \ifLongCites{\cite{grebinski-journal}}{Grebinski and Kucherov~\cite{grebinski-journal}}. They showed that a set of $f'(m)= \Theta(m/\log m)$ random coin-weighing queries $y^1, \ldots, y^{f'(m)}$, sampled from $\{0,1\}^m$ independently and uniformly at random, has, with some positive probability, the property that it distinguishes any two distinct coin-weighing instances in the following sense: For any two distinct vectors $v, w$ with non-negative integer entries such that $\sum_{s\in[m]}{v_s} \leq m/2$ and $\sum_{s\in[m]}{w_s} \leq m/2$, there exists an index $j\in[f'(m)]$ for which $\sum_{s\in[m],y^j_s=1}{v_s}\neq\sum_{s\in[m],y^j_s=1}{w_s}$. It follows by the probabilistic method that, deterministically, there is a set $D\subseteq \{0,1\}^m$ of size at most $f'(m)$ such that the answers to the corresponding coin-weighing queries identify every possible coin-weighing instance. Hence we can replace the $f(m)$ random coin-weighing queries of each round by the $f'(m)$ coin-weighing queries corresponding to the fixed set $D$. It remains to derandomize the choice of $r$ in each round. As before we consider $m:=4n/k'$ blocks of size $k'/4$, where $k'$ is the size of the sets $C_i$ at the beginning of a phase. To make sure that a constant fraction of all queries in a phase satisfy $\eq(z,r)\leq m/2$ (compare line~\ref{Bedingung} of Algorithm~\ref{algo:mastermind}), we ask a set of $k'$ queries such that, for each position $i\in[n]$, every color in $C_i$ is used at position $i$ in exactly one of these queries. (If all sets $C_i$ are equal, this can be achieved by simply asking $k'$ monochromatic queries.) The sum of all returned scores must be exactly $n$, and therefore we cannot get a score of more than $m/2 = 2n/k'$ for more than $k'/2$ queries. In this way we ensure that for at least $k-k'/2=k'/2$ queries we get a score of at most $m/2$. As in the randomized version of our strategy, in each of these $k'/2$ queries at least half of the blocks must be $0$-blocks. We can identify those by the derandomized coin-weighing discussed above. Consider now a fixed block. As it has size $k'/4$, it can be a \emph{non}-0-block in at most $k'/4$ queries. Thus it is a $0$-block in at least $k'/2-k'/4=k'/4$ of the queries. To summarize, we have shown that by asking $k'$ queries of the above form we get at least $k'/2$ queries of score at most $m/2$. For each of them we identify the $0$-blocks by coin-weighing queries. This allows us to exclude at least $k'/4$ colors at each position. I.e., as in the randomized version of our strategy we can reduce the number of colors by a constant factor using only $O(k'\cdot m/\log m)=O(n/\log(4n/k))$ queries. By similar calculations as before, the same asymptotic bounds follow. We abandon the color reduction scheme when $k'$ is a constant. At this point, we can solve the remaining problem in time $O(n)$ by repeatedly using the argument we used to determine the dummy colors in Section~\ref{sec:preliminaries}. Note that all of the above can easily be implemented in polynomial time if we can solve the coin-weighing subproblems in polynomial time. An algorithm for doing the latter is given in the work of \ifLongCites{\cite{Bshouty09}}{Bshouty~\cite{Bshouty09}}. Using this algorithm as a building block, we obtain a deterministic polynomial-time strategy for Codebreaker that achieves the bounds stated in Theorem~\ref{thm:main}.
nodes.statement_short: Replace the random coin-weighing queries by a fixed distinguishing set $D$, and the random $r$ by $k'$ queries exhausting every color at every position.

nodes.name: Query complexities $b(n,k)$ and $bw(n,k)$
nodes.section: 3 Mastermind with Black and White Answer-Pegs
nodes.statement: for all $k, n \in \N$ let us denote by $b(n,k)$ the minimum (taken over all strategies) maximum (taken over all secret codes) expected number of queries needed to find the secret code in a black-peg Mastermind game with $k$ colors and $n$ positions. Similarly, denote by $bw(n,k)$ the corresponding number for the game with black and white answer-pegs.
nodes.statement_short: Minimax expected number of queries to find the code, in the black-peg game ($b$) and in the black/white-peg game ($bw$).

nodes.name: Theorem 4 (black/white versus black-peg complexity)
nodes.section: 3 Mastermind with Black and White Answer-Pegs
nodes.statement: For all $k, n \in \N$ with $k \ge n$, \[bw(n,k) = \Theta(k/n + b(n,n)).\]
nodes.statement_short: For $k\ge n$ the black/white-peg complexity is $\Theta(k/n+b(n,n))$.
conclusions: \[bw(n,k) = \Theta(k/n + b(n,n)).\]

nodes.name: $O(n\log\log n)$ for black/white Mastermind up to $n^2\log\log n$ colors
nodes.section: 3 Mastermind with Black and White Answer-Pegs
nodes.statement: Combining this with Theorem~\ref{thm:main}, we obtain a bound of $O(n\log\log n)$ for black/white Mastermind with $n\leq k \leq n^2\log\log n$ colors, improving all previous bounds in that range.
assumptions: black/white Mastermind with $n\leq k \leq n^2\log\log n$ colors
conclusions: a bound of $O(n\log\log n)$ for black/white Mastermind with $n\leq k \leq n^2\log\log n$ colors

nodes.name: Lemma 5 (simulating black/white play with black pegs)
nodes.section: 3 Mastermind with Black and White Answer-Pegs
nodes.statement: For all $n, k$, \[bw(n,k) \ge b(n,k) - k + 1.\]
conclusions: \[bw(n,k) \ge b(n,k) - k + 1.\]

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 5
nodes.section: 3 Mastermind with Black and White Answer-Pegs
nodes.statement: We show that we can simulate a strategy in the black/white Mastermind game by one receiving only black-pegs answers and using $k-1$ more guesses. Fix a strategy for black/white Mastermind. Our black-peg strategy first asks $k-1$ monochromatic queries. This tells us how often each of the $k$ color arises in the secret code. From now on, we can play the strategy for the black/white game. While we only receive black answer-pegs, we can compute the number of white pegs we would have gotten in the black/white game from the just obtained information on how often each color occurs in the code. With this information available, we can indeed play as in the given strategy for black/white Mastermind.
nodes.statement_short: $k-1$ monochromatic queries reveal every color's multiplicity, after which the white-peg answers can be computed from the black-peg ones.

nodes.name: Corollary 6 ($bw=\Theta(b)$ for $k\le n$)
nodes.section: 3 Mastermind with Black and White Answer-Pegs
nodes.statement: For all $k \le n$, \[bw(n,k) = \Theta(b(n,k)).\]
conclusions: \[bw(n,k) = \Theta(b(n,k)).\]

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 6
nodes.section: 3 Mastermind with Black and White Answer-Pegs
nodes.statement: Obviously, $bw(n,k) \le b(n,k)$ for all $n,k$. If $k = o(n)$, then the information theoretic lower bound $b(n,k) = \Omega(n \log k / \log n)$ is of larger order than $k$, hence the lemma above shows the claim. For $k = \Theta(n)$, note first that both $b(n,k)$ and $bw(n,k)$ are in $\Omega(n)$ due to the information theoretic argument. If $b(n,k) = O(n)$, there is nothing to show. If $b(n,k) = \omega(n)$, we again invoke Lemma~\ref{lem:bw}.
nodes.statement_short: Split into $k=o(n)$, where the information-theoretic bound dominates the $-k+1$ loss, and $k=\Theta(n)$.

nodes.name: The color set $C^*$ of the secret code
nodes.section: 3 Mastermind with Black and White Answer-Pegs
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be the set of all available colors and $k = |C|$. Denote by $z \in C^n$ the secret code chosen by Codemaker. Denote by $C^* := \{z_i \mid i \in [n]\}$ the (unknown) set of colors in $z$.
nodes.statement_short: $C^*$ is the unknown set of colors actually occurring in the secret code $z$.

nodes.name: Three-step Codebreaker strategy for black/white Mastermind
nodes.section: 3 Mastermind with Black and White Answer-Pegs
nodes.statement: (1) Codebreaker first asks roughly $k/n$ guesses containing all colors. Only colors in a guess receiving a positive answer can be part of the secret code, so this reduces the number of colors to be regarded to at most $n^2$. Also, Codebreaker can learn from the answers the cardinality $n'$ of $C^*$, that is, the number of distinct colors in the secret code. (2) By asking an expected number of $\Theta(n')$ (dependent) random queries, Codebreaker learns $n'$ disjoint sets of colors of size at most $n$ such that each color of $C^*$ is contained in exactly one of these sets. Denote by $k'$ the cardinality of a largest of these sets. (3) Given such a family of sets, Codebreaker can learn $C^*$ with an expected number of $b(n', k')$ queries by simulating an optimal black-peg Mastermind strategy. Once $C^*$ is known, an expected number of $b(n,n')$ queries determine the secret code, using an optimal black-peg strategy for $n'$ colors.
nodes.statement_short: Shrink the color pool with $k/n$ color queries, split the survivors into $n'$ singleton-intersecting sets, then run a black-peg strategy twice.
input: Denote by $z \in C^n$ the secret code chosen by Codemaker

nodes.name: Lemma 7 (learning $\col(X)$ with one color query)
nodes.section: 3 Mastermind with Black and White Answer-Pegs
nodes.statement: For an arbitrary set $X$ of at most $n$ colors, let $\col(X) := |C^* \cap X|$, the number of colors of $X$ occurring in the secret code. After a single initial query, Codebreaker can learn $\col(X)$ for any $X$ via a single Mastermind query to be answered by black and white pegs.
nodes.statement_short: After one initial monochromatic query, a single black/white query reveals $|C^*\cap X|$ for any color set $X$ of size $\le n$.
assumptions: For an arbitrary set $X$ of at most $n$ colors
conclusions: Codebreaker can learn $\col(X)$ for any $X$ via a single Mastermind query to be answered by black and white pegs

nodes.name: $\col(X)$
nodes.section: 3 Mastermind with Black and White Answer-Pegs
nodes.statement: let $\col(X) := |C^* \cap X|$, the number of colors of $X$ occurring in the secret code

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 7
nodes.section: 3 Mastermind with Black and White Answer-Pegs
nodes.statement:
As the single initial query, Codebreaker may ask $(1,\ldots,1)$, the code consisting of color~1 only. Denote by $b$ the number of black pegs received (there cannot be a white answer-peg). This is the number of occurrences of color~$1$ in the secret code. Let $X \subseteq C$, $
u := |X| \le n$. To learn $\col(X)$, Codebreaker extends $X$ to a multiset of $n$ colors by adding the color 1 exactly $n-
u$ times and guesses a code arbitrarily composed of this multiset of colors. Let $y$ be the total number of (black and white) answer-pegs received. Then $\col(X) = y - \min\{n-
u,b\}$, if $1 
otin X$ or $b = 0$, and $\col(X) = y - \min\{n-
u,b-1\}$ otherwise.
nodes.statement_short: Pad $X$ with copies of color $1$ to length $n$; the total peg count minus the known contribution of the padding gives $\col(X)$.

nodes.name: Color query
nodes.section: 3 Mastermind with Black and White Answer-Pegs
nodes.statement: To ease the language, we shall call a query determining $\col(X)$ a \emph{color query}.

nodes.name: Lemma 8 (color reduction with $\lceil k/n\rceil$ color queries)
nodes.section: 3 Mastermind with Black and White Answer-Pegs
nodes.statement: With $\lceil k/n \rceil$ color queries, Codebreaker can learn both $|C^*|$ and a superset $C_0$ of $C^*$ consisting of at most $n |C^*|$ colors.
conclusions: Codebreaker can learn both $|C^*|$ and a superset $C_0$ of $C^*$ consisting of at most $n |C^*|$ colors

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 8
nodes.section: 3 Mastermind with Black and White Answer-Pegs
nodes.statement: Let $X_1, \ldots, X_{\lceil k/n \rceil}$ be a partition of $C$ into sets of cardinality at most $n$. By asking the corresponding $\lceil k/n \rceil$ color queries, Codebreaker immediately learns $|C^*| := \sum_{i = 1}^{\lceil k/n \rceil} \col(X_i)$. Also, $C_0 := \bigcup \{X_i \mid \col(X_i) > 0\}$ is the desired superset.
nodes.statement_short: Color-query the parts of a size-$n$ partition of $C$; the answers sum to $|C^*|$ and the positive parts union to $C_0$.

nodes.name: Lemma 9 (splitting $C_0$ into $n'$ singleton-intersecting sets)
nodes.section: 3 Mastermind with Black and White Answer-Pegs
nodes.statement: Assume that Codebreaker knows the number $n' = |C^*|$ of different colors in $z$ as well as a set $C_0 \supseteq C^*$ of colors such that $|C_0| \le n |C^*|$. Then with an expected number of $\Theta(n')$ color queries, Codebreaker can find a family $C_1, \ldots, C_{n'}$ of disjoint subsets of $C_0$, each of size at most $ \lceil |C_0|/n' \rceil \le n$, such that $C^* \subseteq C_1 \cup \ldots \cup C_{n'}$ and $|C^* \cap C_i| = 1$ for all $i \in [n']$.
nodes.statement_short: $\Theta(n')$ random color queries produce disjoint sets $C_1,\dots,C_{n'}$ of size $\le n$ each containing exactly one color of $C^*$.
assumptions: Assume that Codebreaker knows the number $n' = |C^*|$ of different colors in $z$ as well as a set $C_0 \supseteq C^*$ of colors such that $|C_0| \le n |C^*|$
conclusions: Then with an expected number of $\Theta(n')$ color queries, Codebreaker can find a family $C_1, \ldots, C_{n'}$ of disjoint subsets of $C_0$, each of size at most $ \lceil |C_0|/n' \rceil \le n$, such that $C^* \subseteq C_1 \cup \ldots \cup C_{n'}$ and $|C^* \cap C_i| = 1$ for all $i \in [n']$

nodes.name: Algorithm 2: Codebreaker's color-splitting strategy
nodes.section: 3 Mastermind with Black and White Answer-Pegs
nodes.statement: \While{$n' > 0$}{ $k' \assign \lceil |C_0|/n' \rceil$\; Let $C_{n'}$ be a random subset of $C$ with $|C_{n'}| = k'$\; Ask the color query $C_{n'}$\; \If{$\col(C_{n'}) = 1$}{ $C_0 \assign C_0 \setminus C_{n'}$\; $n' \assign n' - 1$\;
nodes.statement_short: Repeatedly draw a random color set of size $\lceil |C_0|/n'\rceil$ and keep it whenever its color query answers $1$.
input: a set $C_0 \supseteq C^*$ of colors such that $|C_0| \le n |C^*|$
the number $n' = |C^*|$ of different colors in $z$
output: a family $C_1, \ldots, C_{n'}$ of disjoint subsets of $C_0$

nodes.name: Lower bound on the probability that $\col(C_{n'})=1$
nodes.section: 3 Mastermind with Black and White Answer-Pegs
nodes.statement_short: A telescoping product bound showing the acceptance probability of a random color set is bounded below by a constant.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 9
nodes.section: 3 Mastermind with Black and White Answer-Pegs
nodes.statement: Roughly speaking, Codebreaker's strategy is to ask color queries having an expected answer of one. With constant probability, such a query contains exactly one color from $C^*$. Below is a precise formulation of this strategy. \begin{algorithm2e} \While{$n' > 0$}{ $k' \assign \lceil |C_0|/n' \rceil$\; Let $C_{n'}$ be a random subset of $C$ with $|C_{n'}| = k'$\; Ask the color query $C_{n'}$\; \If{$\col(C_{n'}) = 1$}{ $C_0 \assign C_0 \setminus C_{n'}$\; $n' \assign n' - 1$\; } } \caption{Codebreaker's strategy} \end{algorithm2e} For the analysis, note first that the value of $k'$ during the application of the above strategy does not increase. In particular, all sets $C_i$ defined and queried have cardinality at most $\lceil |C_0|/n' \rceil \le n$. It is also clear that the above strategy constructs a sequence of disjoint $C_i$ and that for each color occurring in $z$ there is exactly one $C_i$ containing this color. It remains to prove the estimate on the expected number of queries. To this aim, we first note that throughout a run of this strategy, $n'$ is the number of colors of $C^*$ left in $C_0$. Hence the event ``$\col(C_{n'}) = 1$'' occurs with probability \begin{align*} \frac{n' k' (|C_0| - n') \ldots (|C_0| - n' - k' + 2)}{|C_0| \ldots (|C_0| - k' + 1)} &\ge \frac{(|C_0| - n') \ldots (|C_0| - n' - k' + 2)}{(|C_0|-1) \ldots (|C_0| - k' + 1)} \\ & \ge \bigg( \frac{|C_0| - n' - k' + 2}{|C_0| - k' + 1} \bigg)^{k'-1} = \bigg( 1 - \frac{n' - 1}{|C_0| - k' + 1} \bigg)^{k'-1}\\ & \ge \bigg( 1 - \frac{n' - 1}{|C_0| - (|C_0|/n')} \bigg)^{k'-1}\\ & \ge \bigg( 1 - \frac{|C_0| / (k'-1)}{|C_0| - (|C_0|/n')} \bigg)^{k'-1}\\ & \ge \bigg( 1 - \frac{1}{(k'-1)(1 - 1/n')} \bigg)^{k'-1},\\ \end{align*} which is bounded from below by a constant (the later estimates assume $n' \ge 2$; for $n'=1$ the second term of the sequence of inequalities already is one). Consequently, with constant probability the randomly chosen $C_{n'}$ satisfies ``$\col(C_{n'}) = 1$''. Hence after an expected constant number of iterations of the while-loop, such a $C_{n'}$ will be found. Since each such success reduces the value of $n'$ by one, a total expected number of $\Theta(|C^*|)$ iterations suffices to find the desired family of sets $(C_i)_{i \in [n']}$.
nodes.statement_short: Give the sampling loop, argue correctness of the constructed family, then bound the acceptance probability below by a constant.

nodes.name: Lemma 10 (detecting $C^*$ by simulating a black-peg strategy)
nodes.section: 3 Mastermind with Black and White Answer-Pegs
nodes.statement: Let $C_1, \ldots, C_{n'}$ be a family of disjoint subsets of $C$ such that $C^* \subseteq C_1 \cup \ldots \cup C_{n'}$ and $|C^* \cap C_i| = 1$ for all $i \in [n']$. Assume that $k' := \max\{|C_i| \mid i \in [n']\} \le n$. Then Codebreaker can detect $C^*$ using an expected number of $b(n', k')$ color queries.
nodes.statement_short: Given such a family, $b(n',k')$ color queries simulate a black-peg game on $C_1\times\dots\times C_{n'}$ and reveal $C^*$.
assumptions: Let $C_1, \ldots, C_{n'}$ be a family of disjoint subsets of $C$ such that $C^* \subseteq C_1 \cup \ldots \cup C_{n'}$ and $|C^* \cap C_i| = 1$ for all $i \in [n']$
conclusions: Then Codebreaker can detect $C^*$ using an expected number of $b(n', k')$ color queries

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 10
nodes.section: 3 Mastermind with Black and White Answer-Pegs
nodes.statement: Let $z' \in C_1 \times \ldots \times C_{n'}$ be the unique such string consisting of colors in $C^*$ only. Note that in black-peg Mastermind, the particular sets of colors used at each position are irrelevant. Hence there is a strategy for Codebreaker to detect $z'$ using an expected number of $b(n',k')$ guesses from $C_1 \times \ldots \times C_{n'}$ and receiving black-peg answers only. We now show that for each such query, there is a corresponding color query in the $(n,k)$ black/white Mastermind game giving the same answer. Hence we may simulate the black-peg game searching for $z'$ by such color queries. Since $z'$ contains all colors of $C^*$ and no other colors, once found, it reveals the set of colors occurring in the original secret code $z$. Let $y' \in C_1 \times \ldots \times C_{n'}$ be a query in the black-peg Mastermind game searching for $z'$. For each position $i\in[n']$, we have $z'_i=y'_i$ if and only if $y_i'\in C_i$ is the unique color from $C_i$ that is in $C^*$. As moreover the sets $(C_i)_{i\in [n']}$ are disjoint, we have $\eq(z',y') = \col(\{y'_1, \ldots, y'_{n'}\})$, and we can obtain this value (i.e., the black-peg answer for the guess $y'$ relative to $z'$) by a color query relative to $z$.
nodes.statement_short: Every black-peg query for the induced string $z'$ has an equal-answer color query in the original game, since $\eq(z',y')=\col(\{y'_1,\dots,y'_{n'}\})$.

nodes.name: More efficient determination of $C^*$ when $k \ll n^2$
nodes.section: 3 Mastermind with Black and White Answer-Pegs
nodes.statement: Note that if our only goal is to find out $C^*$, then for $k \ll n^2$ we can be more efficient by asking more color queries in Lemma~\ref{lemreduce}, leading to a smaller set $C_0$, to smaller sets $C_i$ in Lemma~\ref{lempartition}, and thus to a smaller $k'$ value in Lemma~\ref{lemlast}. Since this will not affect the asymptotic bound for the total numbers of queries used in the black/white-peg game, we omit the details.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4
nodes.section: 3 Mastermind with Black and White Answer-Pegs
nodes.statement: The upper bound follows easily from applying Lemmas~\ref{lemfirst} to~\ref{lemlast}, which show that Codebreaker can detect the set $C^*$ of colors arising in the secret code $z$ with an expected number of $1 + \lceil k/n \rceil + O(n) + b(n,n)$ guesses. Since $|C^*| \le n$, he can now use a strategy for black-peg Mastermind and determine $z$ with another expected number of $b(n,n)$ guesses. Note that $b(n,n) = \Omega(n)$, so this proves the upper bound. We argue that this upper bound is optimal apart from constant factors. Assume first that the secret code is a random monochromatic string (Codemaker may even announce this). Fix a (possibly randomized) strategy for Codebreaker. With probability at least 1/2, this strategy does not use the particular color in any of the first $k/(2n)$ guesses. It then also did not guess the correct code. Hence the expected number of queries necessary to find the code is at least $k/(4n)$. We finally show that for $k \ge n$, also the $b(n,n)$ term cannot be avoided. By the information theoretic argument, there is nothing to show if $b(n,n) = \Theta(n)$. Hence assume $b(n,n) = \omega(n)$. We will show $bw(n,k) + n + 1 \ge bw(n,n)$. The claim then follows from $bw(n,n) = \Theta(b(n,n))$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:bw}). We show that we can solve the $k=n$ color Mastermind game by asking $n+1$ preliminary queries and then simulating a strategy for black/white Mastermind with $n$ positions and $k > n$. As in Section~\ref{sec:preliminaries}, we use $n+1$ queries to learn for each position whether it has color $1$ or not. We then simulate a given strategy for $k > n$ colors as follows. In a $k$-color query, replace all colors greater than $n$ by color $1$. Since we know the positions of the pegs in color $1$, we can reduce the answers by the contribution of these additional 1-pegs in the query. This gives the answer we would have gotten in reply to the original query (since the secret code does not contain colors higher than $n$). Consequently, we can now simulate the $k$-color strategy in an $n$-color Mastermind game.
nodes.statement_short: Chain Lemmas 7--10 for the upper bound; for the lower bound use a random monochromatic code and a simulation showing $bw(n,k)+n+1\ge bw(n,n)$.

nodes.name: What to measure for non-adaptive strategies
nodes.statement: When analyzing the performance of non-adaptive strategies, it is not very meaningful to ask for the number of queries needed until the secret code is queried for the first time. Instead we ask for the number of queries needed to \emph{identify} it.

nodes.name: Erd\H os--R\'enyi bound for two-color Mastermind
nodes.origin_citation: Erd\H os and R\'enyi 1963; Lindstr\"om 1964, 1965; Cantor and Mills 1966
nodes.statement: In their work on the $2$-color black-peg version of Mastermind, \ifLongCites{\cite{Erd63}}{Erd{\H{o}}s and R\'enyi~\cite{Erd63}} showed that random guessing needs, with high probability, $(2+o(1)) n /\log n$ queries to identify the secret code, and that this is in fact best possible among \emph{non-adaptive} winning strategies. The upper bound was derandomized by \ifLongCites{\cite{Lindstroem64,Lindstroem65}}{Lindstr\"om~\cite{Lindstroem64,Lindstroem65}} and, independently, by \ifLongCites{\cite{CantorM66}}{Cantor and Mills~\cite{CantorM66}}. That is, for 2-color black-pegs Mastermind a deterministic non-adaptive winning strategy using $(2+o(1)) n /\log n$ guesses exists, and no non-adaptive strategy can do better.
nodes.statement_short: For $k=2$, random guessing identifies the code in $(2+o(1))n/\log n$ queries, this is non-adaptively optimal, and it can be derandomized.
conclusions: random guessing needs, with high probability, $(2+o(1)) n /\log n$ queries to identify the secret code, and that this is in fact best possible among \emph{non-adaptive} winning strategies
a deterministic non-adaptive winning strategy using $(2+o(1)) n /\log n$ guesses exists, and no non-adaptive strategy can do better

nodes.name: Adaptive lower bound for two-color Mastermind
nodes.origin_citation: information-theoretic argument; cf. Erd\H os and R\'enyi 1963
nodes.statement: For adaptive strategies, only a weaker lower bound of $(1+o(1))n /\log n$ is known. This bound results from the information-theoretic argument mentioned in Section~\ref{sec:previous}.
conclusions: only a weaker lower bound of $(1+o(1))n /\log n$ is known

nodes.name: Is there an adaptive strategy matching $(1+o(1))n/\log n$?
nodes.statement: It remains a major open problem whether there exists an adaptive strategy that achieves this bound. In fact, it is not even known whether adaptive strategies can outperform the random guessing strategy by \emph{any} constant factor.
nodes.statement_short: Whether adaptive strategies beat random guessing for two-color Mastermind, even by a constant factor, is unknown.

nodes.name: Adaptive strategies separate from non-adaptive ones for $k=\Theta(n)$
nodes.statement: Here in this section we prove that for Mastermind with $k=\Theta(n)$ colors, adaptive strategies are indeed more powerful than non-adaptive ones, and outperform them even in order of magnitude. More precisely, we show that any non-adaptive strategy needs $\Omega(n \log n)$ guesses. Since we know from Section~\ref{sec:nloglogn} that adaptively we can achieve a bound of $O(n \log \log n)$, this separates the performance of non-adaptive strategies from that of adaptive ones. Our result answers a question left open in~\cite{Goddard03}.
nodes.statement_short: For $k=\Theta(n)$, non-adaptive strategies need $\Omega(n\log n)$ guesses while adaptive ones need only $O(n\log\log n)$.
conclusions: any non-adaptive strategy needs $\Omega(n \log n)$ guesses
this separates the performance of non-adaptive strategies from that of adaptive ones

nodes.name: Deterministic and randomized non-adaptive strategies
nodes.statement: A deterministic non-adaptive strategy is a fixed ordering $x^1, x^2, \ldots, x^{k^n}$ of all possible guesses, i.e., the elements of $[k]^n$. A randomized non-adaptive strategy is a probability distribution over such orderings. For a given secret code $z\in[k]^n$, we ask for the smallest index $j$ such that the queries $x^1, \ldots, x^j$ together with their answers $\eq(z,x^1), \ldots, \eq(z,x^j)$ uniquely determine $z$.
nodes.statement_short: A non-adaptive strategy is a fixed (or randomly drawn) ordering of all guesses, scored by how many prefixes are needed to pin down the code.
nodes.genus: a fixed ordering $x^1, x^2, \ldots, x^{k^n}$ of all possible guesses

nodes.name: Static Mastermind
nodes.statement: Mastermind with non-adaptive strategies is also referred to as \emph{static} Mastermind~\cite{Goddard03}.

nodes.name: Theorem 11 (lower bound for non-adaptive strategies)
nodes.statement: For any (randomized or deterministic) non-adaptive strategy for black-peg Mastermind with $n$ positions and $k$ colors, the expected number of queries needed to determine a secret code $z$ sampled uniformly at random from $[k]^n$ is $\Omega \left( \frac{n \log k}{\max\{\log(n/k), 1\}} \right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Every non-adaptive strategy needs $\Omega(n\log k/\max\{\log(n/k),1\})$ queries in expectation on a uniformly random code.
assumptions: For any (randomized or deterministic) non-adaptive strategy for black-peg Mastermind with $n$ positions and $k$ colors
a secret code $z$ sampled uniformly at random from $[k]^n$
conclusions: the expected number of queries needed to determine a secret code $z$ sampled uniformly at random from $[k]^n$ is $\Omega \left( \frac{n \log k}{\max\{\log(n/k), 1\}} \right)$

nodes.name: A hard secret code exists for every non-adaptive strategy
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm:nonadaptive} shows, in particular, that for any non-adaptive strategy there exists a secret code $z\in[k]^n$ which can only be identified after $\Omega\left(n \log k / \max\{\log(n/k), 1\} \right)$ queries. For $k\geq n$, this is an improvement of $\Theta(\log n)$ over the information-theoretic lower bound mentioned in the introduction.
nodes.statement_short: Every non-adaptive strategy has a worst-case code needing $\Omega(n\log k/\max\{\log(n/k),1\})$ queries, beating the information-theoretic bound by $\Theta(\log n)$ when $k\ge n$.
conclusions: there exists a secret code $z\in[k]^n$ which can only be identified after $\Omega\left(n \log k / \max\{\log(n/k), 1\} \right)$ queries
For $k\geq n$, this is an improvement of $\Theta(\log n)$ over the information-theoretic lower bound

nodes.name: Entropy intuition behind Theorem 11
nodes.statement: To give an intuition for the correctness of Theorem~\ref{thm:nonadaptive}, note that for a uniformly chosen secret code $z \in [k]^n$, for any single fixed guess $x$ of a non-adaptive strategy the answer $\eq(z,x)$ is binomially distributed with parameters $n$ and $1/k$. That is, $\eq(z,x)$ will typically be within the interval $n/k \pm O(\sqrt{n/k})$. Hence, we can typically encode the answer using $\log( O(\sqrt{n/k})) = O(\log(n/k))$ bits. Or, stated differently, our `information gain' is usually $O(\log(n/k))$ bits. Since the secret code `holds $n \log k$ bits of information', we would expect that we have to make $\Omega(n \log k / \log(n/k))$ guesses.
nodes.statement_short: Each answer is binomial and so carries only $O(\log(n/k))$ bits, while the code holds $n\log k$ bits.

nodes.name: Entropy
nodes.statement: For a discrete random variable $Z$ over a domain $D$, the \emph{entropy} of $Z$ is defined by $H(Z) := - \sum_{z \in D} \Pr[Z = z] \log(\Pr[Z=z])$.

nodes.name: Entropy of a fair versus a biased coin toss
nodes.statement: Intuitively speaking, the entropy measures the amount of information that the random variable $Z$ carries. If $Z$ for example corresponds to a random coin toss with $\Pr[\text{`heads'}] = \Pr[\text{`tails'}] = 1/2$, then $Z$ carries 1 bit of information. However, a biased coin toss with $\Pr[\text{`heads'}] = 2/3$ carries less (roughly 0.918 bits of) information since we know that the outcome of heads is more likely.

nodes.name: (E1) Entropy does not increase under deterministic maps
nodes.statement: If $Z$ is determined by the outcome of $Y$, i.e., $Z = f(Y)$ for a deterministic function $f$, then we have $H(Z) \le H(Y)$.
assumptions: If $Z$ is determined by the outcome of $Y$, i.e., $Z = f(Y)$ for a deterministic function $f$
conclusions: $H(Z) \le H(Y)$

nodes.name: (E2) Subadditivity of entropy
nodes.statement: We have $H((Z, Y)) \le H(Z) + H(Y)$.
conclusions: $H((Z, Y)) \le H(Z) + H(Y)$

nodes.name: Equality in (E2) characterizes independence
nodes.statement: The inequality in (E2) holds with equality if and only if the two variables $Z$ and $Y$ are independent.

nodes.name: Lemma 12 (random guessing for $k=\Theta(n)$)
nodes.statement: For black-peg Mastermind with $n$ positions and $k=\Theta(n)$ colors, the random guessing strategy needs an expected number of $O(n \log n)$ queries to determine an arbitrary fixed code $z\in[k]^n$. Furthermore, for a large enough constant $C$, $Cn\log n$ queries suffice with probability $1-o(1)$.
nodes.statement_short: For $k=\Theta(n)$, random guessing determines any fixed code within $O(n\log n)$ queries in expectation and w.h.p.
assumptions: For black-peg Mastermind with $n$ positions and $k=\Theta(n)$ colors
conclusions: the random guessing strategy needs an expected number of $O(n \log n)$ queries to determine an arbitrary fixed code $z\in[k]^n$
$Cn\log n$ queries suffice with probability $1-o(1)$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 12
nodes.statement: We can easily eliminate colors whenever we receive a $0$-answer. For every position $i \in [n]$ we need to eliminate $k-1$ potential colors. This can be seen as having $n$ parallel coupon collectors, each of which needs to collect $k-1$ coupons. The probability that for a random guess we get an answer of $0$ is $(1-1/k)^n$, i.e., constant. Conditional on a $0$-answer, the color excluded at each position is sampled uniformly from all $k-1$ colors that are wrong at that particular position. Thus the probability that at least one of the $k-1$ wrong colors at one fixed position is \emph{not} eliminated by the first $t$ $0$-answers is bounded by $(k-1)(1-\frac{1}{k-1})^t\leq k e^{-t/k}$. Let now $T$ denote the random variable that counts the number of $0$-answers needed to determine the secret code. By a union bound over all $n$ positions, we have $\Pr[T\geq t]\leq nk\e^{-t/k}=\Theta(n^2)\cdot e^{-\Theta(t/n)}$. It follows by routine calculations that $\mathbb{E}[T]=O(n\log n)$ and $\Pr[T\geq Cn\log n]=o(1)$ for $C$ large enough. As a random query returns a value of $0$ with constant probability, the same bounds also hold for the total number of queries needed.
nodes.statement_short: View the elimination as $n$ parallel coupon collectors and take a union bound over positions on the number of $0$-answers.

nodes.name: Explicit non-adaptive polynomial-time strategy
nodes.statement: It remains an open question to find an explicit non-adaptive polynomial-time strategy that achieves this bound.

nodes.name: Theorem 13 (matching deterministic non-adaptive strategy)
nodes.statement: There exists $n_0 \in \mathbb N$ and a constant $C > 0$ such that for every $n \ge n_0$ and $k \le n$ there exists a deterministic non-adaptive strategy for black-peg Mastermind with $n$ positions and $k$ colors that uses at most $C \frac{n \log k}{\max \{ \log(n/k), 1 \}}$ queries.
nodes.statement_short: For all $k\le n$ there is a deterministic non-adaptive strategy using $O(n\log k/\max\{\log(n/k),1\})$ queries, matching Theorem 11.
conclusions: there exists a deterministic non-adaptive strategy for black-peg Mastermind with $n$ positions and $k$ colors that uses at most $C \frac{n \log k}{\max \{ \log(n/k), 1 \}}$ queries

nodes.name: Difference pattern
nodes.statement: Based on this observation we define (similar to~\cite{Chvatal83}) a \emph{difference pattern} to be a set of indices $I \subseteq [n]$ together with two lists of colors $(c_i)_{i \in I}, (c'_i)_{i \in I}$ such that $c_i \neq c'_i$ for every $i \in I$.
nodes.statement_short: An index set $I$ carrying two everywhere-differing color lists, abstracting a pair of distinct secret codes.
nodes.genus: a set of indices $I \subseteq [n]$ together with two lists of colors $(c_i)_{i \in I}, (c'_i)_{i \in I}$

nodes.name: Difference pattern corresponding to $z$ and $z'$
nodes.statement: For every two distinct secret codes $z, z' \in [k]^n$ we define the difference pattern corresponding to $z$ and $z'$ to be the set $I(z,z') := \{ i \in [n] : z_i \neq z'_i \}$ together with the lists $(z_i)_{i \in I}$ and $(z'_i)_{i \in I}$.
nodes.definiendum: the difference pattern corresponding to $z$ and $z'$

nodes.name: A query splits a difference pattern
nodes.statement: We say that a query $x \in [k]^n$ \emph{splits} a difference pattern given by $I$, $(c_i)_{i \in I}$, and $(c'_i)_{i \in I}$ if \[ | \{ i \in I : x_i = c_i \} | \neq | \{ i \in I : x_i = c'_i \} |. \]
nodes.statement_short: A query splits a pattern when it agrees with the two color lists on differently many indices of $I$.
differentia: | \{ i \in I : x_i = c_i \} | \neq | \{ i \in I : x_i = c'_i \} |

nodes.name: Size of a difference pattern
nodes.statement: The \emph{size} of a difference pattern $I$, $(c_i)_{i \in I}$, $(c'_i)_{i \in I}$ is the cardinality of $I$.

nodes.name: $p(d,k)$, the non-splitting probability
nodes.statement: Note that for fixed $k$, the probability that a particular difference pattern is \emph{not} split by a randomly chosen query only depends on its size. Let $p(d,k)$ denote this probability for a difference pattern of size $d$.
nodes.statement_short: $p(d,k)$ is the probability that a uniformly random query fails to split a size-$d$ difference pattern.

nodes.name: Splitting every difference pattern identifies the code
nodes.statement: It is now easy to see that if a set of $N$ queries has the property that every possible difference pattern is split by at least one query from that set, then these $N$ queries together with the answers deterministically identify Codebreaker's secret code.
assumptions: if a set of $N$ queries has the property that every possible difference pattern is split by at least one query
conclusions: these $N$ queries together with the answers deterministically identify Codebreaker's secret code

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 13
nodes.statement:
The idea is to use a probabilistic method type of argument, i.e., we show that, for an appropriately chosen constant $C > 0$ and $n$ large enough, a set of $N = C  rac{n \log k}{\max \{ \log(n/k), 1 \}}$ random guesses with positive probability identifies every possible secret code. (In fact, we will show that such a set of queries has this property with high probability.) If a set $X=\{x^{(i)} \mid i \in N\}$ of queries distinguishes any two possible secret codes $z, z'$, then there must exist for each such pair $z
eq z'$ a query $x \in X$ with $\eq(z,x) 
eq \eq(z',x)$. In particular we must have $| \{ i \in I(z,z') : x_i = z_i \} | 
eq | \{ i \in I(z,z') : x_i = z'_i \} |$ for $I(z,z') := \{ i \in [n] : z_i 
eq z'_i \}$. Based on this observation we define (similar to~\cite{Chvatal83}) a \emph{difference pattern} to be a set of indices $I \subseteq [n]$ together with two lists of colors $(c_i)_{i \in I}, (c'_i)_{i \in I}$ such that $c_i 
eq c'_i$ for every $i \in I$. For every two distinct secret codes $z, z' \in [k]^n$ we define the difference pattern corresponding to $z$ and $z'$ to be the set $I(z,z') := \{ i \in [n] : z_i 
eq z'_i \}$ together with the lists $(z_i)_{i \in I}$ and $(z'_i)_{i \in I}$. We say that a query $x \in [k]^n$ \emph{splits} a difference pattern given by $I$, $(c_i)_{i \in I}$, and $(c'_i)_{i \in I}$ if \[ | \{ i \in I : x_i = c_i \} | 
eq | \{ i \in I : x_i = c'_i \} |. \] It is now easy to see that if a set of $N$ queries has the property that every possible difference pattern is split by at least one query from that set, then these $N$ queries together with the answers deterministically identify Codebreaker's secret code. Note that for fixed $k$, the probability that a particular difference pattern is \emph{not} split by a randomly chosen query only depends on its size. Let $p(d,k)$ denote this probability for a difference pattern of size $d$. The probability that there exists a difference pattern that is not split by any of the $N$ random queries is at most \[ \sum_{d=1}^{n}  inom nd (k(k-1))^d (p(d,k))^N . \] In order to show that this probability is at most $1/n$ it thus suffices to prove that for every $d \in [n]$ we have  egin{equation}  inom nd (k(k-1))^d (p(d,k))^N < n^{-2} . \end{equation} We first take a closer look at $p(d,k)$. Observe that if a query $x$ does \emph{not} split a fixed difference pattern $I$, $(c_i)_{i \in I}$, $(c'_i)_{i \in I}$, then $x_i$ must agree with $c_i$ on exactly half of the positions in $I':=\{ i \in I \mid x_i \in \{c_i,c'_i\} \}$, and it must agree with $c'_i$ on the other positions in $I'$. In particular, the size of $I'$ must be even. More precisely, we have  egin{align*} p(d,k) & = \sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor d/2 floor}  inom d{2i}  inom{2i}i \left(  rac 1k ight)^{2i} \left(1 -  rac2k ight)^{d-2i} \ & = \sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor d/2 floor}  inom d{2i} \left(  rac 2k ight)^{2i} \left(1 -  rac2k ight)^{d-2i}  inom{2i}{i} 2^{-2i} . \end{align*} Note that $ inom{2i}i 2^{-2i} \le 1/2$ for every $i \ge 1$, and $1-x \leq e^{-x}$ for all $x\in \R$. Hence,  egin{align*} p(d,k) & \le \left( 1 -  rac 2k ight)^d +  rac12 \sum_{j=1}^{d}  inom dj \left(  rac2k ight)^{j} \left( 1 -  rac2k ight)^{d-j} \ & = 1 -  rac12 \left(1 - \left(1 -  rac2k ight)^d ight) \ & \le \exp \left( -  rac12 \left(1 - e^{-  rac{2d}{k}} ight) ight). \end{align*} It follows that  egin{equation} \ln  rac 1{p(d,k)} \ge  rac12 \left( 1 - e^{-  rac{2d}{k}} ight) . \end{equation} We now split the proof into two cases, $k \ge cn$ and $k < cn$ where $c$ is a sufficiently small constant. Hence, the bound claimed in Theorem~ef{thm:non-adaptive-lb} evaluates to $O(n \log n)$ in this case. It thus suffices to show that there exists a constant $C > 0$ such that $N = C n \log n$ queries already identify every secret code with high probability. We show $n^{5d}(p(d,k))^N < 1$ for every $d \in [n]$, which clearly implies~\eqref{eq:non-adaptive-ultimate-goal}. In fact, we show the equivalent inequality  egin{equation}  rac{N}{5d} \ln  rac{1}{p(d,k)} > \ln n. \end{equation} Using~\eqref{eq:non-adaptive-pdk} we obtain  egin{equation}  rac{N}{5d} \ln  rac{1}{p(d,k)} \ge  rac{N}{10}  rac{1-e^{- rac{2d}{k}}}{d}. \end{equation} Using that $d \mapsto (1-e^{-2d/k})/d$ is a decreasing function in $d$ we can continue with \[  rac{N}{5d} \ln  rac{1}{p(d,k)} \ge  rac{N}{10}  rac{(1-e^{- rac{2n}{k}})}{n}, \] which is clearly larger than $\ln n$ for any $N >  rac{10}{(1-e^{-2}) \log e} n \log n$. Hence for such $N$ we have~\eqref{eq:non-adaptive-case1} which settles this case. 	extbf{Case 2.} $k < c n$. In this case we need to be more careful in our analysis since in our claimed bound the factor $\log(n/k)$ might be large and the factor $\log k$ might be substantially smaller than $\log n$. In what follows, we regard only the case $k \ge 3$; the case $k=2$ has already been solved, cf.~\cite{Erd63}. We first consider difference patterns of size $d \le  rac{n \log k}{\log(n/k) \log n}$. As in Case 1 we show that~\eqref{eq:non-adaptive-case1} holds for these patterns. Observe that~\eqref{eq:non-adaptive-case1-step1} holds again in this case. Since the function $d \mapsto (1-e^{-2d/k})/d$ is decreasing in $d$ and since $d \le  rac{n \log k}{\log(n/k) \log n}$ we obtain  egin{equation}  rac{N}{5d} \ln  rac{1}{p(d,k)} \ge  rac{N}{10}  rac{(1-e^{- rac{2n \log k}{k \log(n/k) \log n}}) \log(n/k) \log n}{n \log k}. \end{equation} Next we bound the exponent $ rac{n \log k}{k \log(n/k) \log n}$ in the previous expression. Note that the derivative of $ rac{n \log k}{k \log(n/k) \log n}$ with respect to $k$ is  egin{equation}  rac{ n ( \log n - \ln(2) \log k \log (n/k))}{\ln(2) k^2 \log n \log^2(n/k)}. \end{equation} We now show that this expression is less than 0 for $3 \le k \le n/4$. Indeed, observe that by setting $g(k) = \ln(2) \log k \log(n/k)$ we have for $n$ large enough that $g(3) = \ln(2) \log(3) \log (n/3) > 1.09 \log(n) - 3.3 > \log n$ and $g(n/4) = 2\ln(2) \log(n/4)>\log n$. Moreover, observe that \[ g'(k) =  rac{\log n - \log(k^2)}{k}. \] From this one easily sees that the function $g$ has a local maximum at $k=\sqrt{n}$ as its only extremal point in the interval in the interval $3 \le k \le n/4$. Hence $g(k) > \log n$ for every $3 \le k \le n/4$ and thus \eqref{eq:non-adaptive-exponent} is negative. Hence, $ rac{n \log k}{k \log(n/k) \log n}$ is a decreasing function in $k$ and we have $ rac{n \log k}{k \log(n/k) \log n} \ge  rac{1}{c \log(1/c)} \left(1 +  rac{\log c}{\log n} ight) \ge 1$ for $n$ large enough. With this we can continue~\eqref{eq:non-adaptive-continue-bla} with \[  rac{N}{5d} \ln  rac{1}{p(d,k)} \ge  rac{1-e^{-2}}{10}  rac{N \log(n/k) \log n}{n \log k}, \] which is certainly larger than $\ln n$ for any $N \ge  rac{10}{(1-e^{-2}) \log e}  rac{n \log k}{\log(n/k)}$. This settles the case $k<cn$ for all $d \le  rac{n \log k}{\log(n/k) \log n}$. In the remainder of this proof we consider the case $k<cn$ and $d \ge  rac{n \log k}{\log(n/k) \log n}$. For such $d$ we establish the inequality $2^n k^{2n} (p(d,k))^N < n^{-2}$ which clearly implies~\eqref{eq:non-adaptive-ultimate-goal}. As done previously, we actually show the equivalent inequality  egin{equation} N \log  rac1{p(d,k)} > 2 n \log k + n + 2 \log n. \end{equation} First observe that $ inom{2i}{i} 2^{-2i} \le 1/\sqrt{i}$ for every $i \ge 1$. We denote by $\mathcal Bin(n,p)$ a binomially dsitributed random variable with parameters $n$ and $p$. With this, we obtain  egin{align*} p(d,k) & \le \sum_{j = 0}^{\lfloor d/k floor}  inom dj \left(  rac 2k ight)^j \left( 1 -  rac 2k ight)^{d-j} + \left(  rac dk ight)^{-1/2} \sum_{j = \lfloor d/k floor + 1}^{n}  inom dj \left(  rac 2k ight)^j \left( 1 -  rac 2k ight)^{d-j} \ & = \Pr \left[ \mathcal Bin \left( d, rac 2k ight) \le  rac{d}{k} ight] + \left(  rac dk ight)^{-1/2} \sum_{j = \lfloor d/k floor + 1}^{n}  inom dj \left(  rac 2k ight)^j \left( 1 -  rac 2k ight)^{d-j} . \end{align*} Using the Chernoff bound $\Pr[ \mathcal Bin(n,p) \le (1 - \delta) np] \le \left(  rac{e^{-\delta}}{(1-\delta)^{1-\delta}}ight)^{np}$ we obtain \[ \Pr \left[ \mathcal Bin \left( d, rac 2k ight) \le  rac{d}{k} ight] \le \left(  rac{e^{-1/2}}{\left( 1/2 ight)^{1/2}} ight)^{2d/k} = \left(  rac 2e ight)^{d/k}. \] Hence, we have \[ p(d,k) \le \left(  rac 2e ight)^{d/k} + \left(  rac dk ight)^{-1/2} . \] It is not hard to see that the function \[ f(k) =  rac{\left(  rac2e ight)^{d/k}}{\left(  rac dk ight)^{-1/2}} \] attains its maximum at $k = 2(1 - \ln 2)d$ and that $f(2(1-\ln 2)d) \le 1$.
